title: Gerunds and Infinitives
intro: In English, one verb can be followed by another verb in different forms. Learn when to use a gerund (verb + -ing) and when to use an infinitive (to + base verb). The first verb or expression often determines the form of the next verb.

sections.heading: 1. What is a gerund?
sections.text: A gerund is a verb ending in -ing that works like a noun. It can name an activity, action or experience.
examples: Swimming is good exercise.
I enjoy reading novels.
She is interested in learning English.

sections.heading: 2. What is an infinitive?
sections.text: An infinitive is usually formed with to + the base form of a verb, such as to eat, to study or to improve.
examples: I want to improve my English.
Patrick decided to study harder.
We came to help our friends.

sections.heading: 3. Gerunds as the subject of a sentence
sections.text: A gerund or gerund phrase can come at the beginning of a sentence and act as its subject. A gerund subject normally takes a singular verb.
examples: Running is a great workout.
Reading new books helps you learn vocabulary.
Eating too much sugar can damage your teeth.

sections.heading: 4. Gerunds after certain verbs
sections.text: Some verbs are normally followed by a gerund. Learn the verb and its pattern together: enjoy doing, avoid doing, finish doing, keep doing and practise doing.
examples: I enjoy reading novels.
Patrick finished cleaning his room.
The students practise speaking English every day.

sections.heading: 5. Gerund phrases after verbs
sections.text: A gerund phrase includes the -ing form and any words that complete its meaning. The extra words do not change the gerund pattern.
examples: I enjoy shopping with my friends.
My parents prefer eating dinner at home.
She avoids using her phone during lessons.

sections.heading: 6. Gerunds after the verb be
sections.text: A gerund can follow is, are, was or were to identify an activity, hobby, duty or mistake.
examples: My favourite hobby is hiking.
One of your duties is taking notes during meetings.
His biggest mistake was trusting the wrong person.

sections.heading: 7. Gerunds after verbs of perception
sections.text: After verbs such as see, hear, watch and feel, an object can be followed by a gerund to describe an action in progress.
examples: I saw you talking to the manager.
We heard the neighbours arguing last night.
She felt an insect crawling on her arm.

sections.heading: 8. Gerunds after possessives
sections.text: A possessive adjective or possessive noun can come before a gerund to show who performs the activity.
examples: He doesn't enjoy my singing.
Her cooking is simple but delicious.
The baby's crying woke me up.

sections.heading: 9. Gerunds after prepositions
sections.text: When a verb follows a preposition, it normally takes the -ing form. Common examples include after, before, without and by.
examples: They left without saying goodbye.
I went to the gym after finishing my work.
You can improve your English by taking a course.

sections.heading: 10. Gerunds after phrasal verbs and expressions
sections.text: Some phrasal verbs and fixed expressions are followed by a gerund. Notice that to in look forward to is a preposition, so it is followed by -ing.
examples: She kept on trying despite the difficulties.
We ended up cancelling the picnic because of the bad weather.
I look forward to meeting you next week.

sections.heading: 11. Infinitives after certain verbs
sections.text: Some verbs are normally followed by an infinitive. Common examples include want, hope, decide, plan, need and promise.
examples: I want to improve my English.
Patrick decided to study harder.
Do you hope to participate in the competition?

sections.heading: 12. Infinitives after an object
sections.text: Some verbs follow the pattern verb + object + to + base verb. The object tells us who is expected, encouraged or asked to do the action.
examples: They encouraged the students to speak English.
The teacher asked Moussa to explain his answer.
The manager expects us to arrive on time.

sections.heading: 13. Infinitives to express purpose
sections.text: An infinitive can explain the purpose of an action. It often answers the question Why?
examples: I study hard to pass my examinations.
She saves money to buy a laptop.
The government built a clinic to improve public health.

sections.heading: 14. Infinitives after adjectives
sections.text: An infinitive often follows an adjective to explain how easy, difficult, important or enjoyable an action is.
examples: It is important to practise every day.
Mathematics is difficult to understand.
The football match was exciting to watch.

sections.heading: 15. Infinitives after question words
sections.text: Question words such as what, where, when, who, how and which can be followed by an infinitive in certain expressions.
examples: I don't know how to solve this problem.
Please tell me where to meet you.
She hasn't decided what to study at university.

sections.heading: 16. Infinitives after enough and words such as nothing
sections.text: An infinitive can follow expressions such as adjective + enough, enough + noun, and nothing/something + to do.
examples: She is old enough to travel alone.
There is nothing to worry about.
We have enough money to buy the tickets.

sections.heading: 17. Infinitives after too + adjective
sections.text: The pattern too + adjective/adverb + to + verb often expresses a limitation or problem.
examples: The bag is too heavy to carry.
He was too tired to continue working.
The water is too hot to drink.

sections.heading: 18. Verbs that can take both forms
sections.text: Some verbs can take a gerund or an infinitive. Sometimes the meaning is similar; with verbs such as remember, stop and try, the meaning can change.
examples: I remember meeting our new teacher. (I remember a past event.)
Remember to lock the door. (Do not forget this task.)
He stopped to answer the phone. (He paused another activity.)

tip: Learn each verb together with its usual pattern: enjoy doing, decide to do, without doing and important to do. After a preposition, use -ing. To explain purpose, use to + base verb. Remember that some verbs can take both forms, sometimes with a change in meaning.
